title: Map Scale Ground Distance Calculator
description: Convert a ground distance back onto the map with the Map Scale Ground Distance Calculator — how many centimetres at 1:25,000 or 1:50,000? Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 10 km ground leg plots as exactly 20.0 cm on a 1:50,000 sheet — but as 40.0 cm on a 1:25,000 sheet, which is why the detailed map needs a bigger table.
quick_answer: The Map Scale Ground Distance Calculator runs the conversion backwards: given a ground distance and a map scale, it tells you how long that distance is on paper. Enter kilometres (or miles) and a denominator of 50,000 and read the centimetres — the check behind route cards and plan drawings.

body.t: A 12.5 km leg: at 1:50,000 it is 25.0 cm of paper; at 1:25,000, 50.0 cm — longer than most folded sheets show at once. The arithmetic explains the walker's preference for the smaller scale on long days.
At 1:10,000, every kilometre is 10.0 cm. A 350 m school frontage must therefore draw as 3.5 cm — a figure a planning officer can verify with a school ruler, which is the point of the convention.

faq: How is this different from the Map Scale Calculator?
Direction. That tool turns a paper measurement into ground distance; this one turns a ground distance into its paper length. Route planning uses both, at different moments.
What denominator do I enter for 1:50,000?
50000 — the number after the colon. The calculator divides your ground distance by it, in consistent units, and reports centimetres.
Yes — the ratio arithmetic is unit-agnostic as long as the ground unit is converted before dividing. The table on this page is metric; the calculator handles the unit you bring.
Why does my measured drawing not match?
Resizing is the usual culprit: a photocopy or PDF printed at 'fit to page' quietly changes the scale. Recover the effective denominator from a known feature and use that.
Is this useful for screen maps?
Less directly — screens zoom continuously, so 'scale' is nominal. The scale bar on a digital map is the honest reference there; this calculator serves print, where scale is fixed.
Exact ratio arithmetic. The practical limit is the ruler and the print, not the division.
What scale should a route card use?
The scale of the sheet the walker carries — the whole point is that card and map agree. Convert with that denominator, whatever it is.
